extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, editorial board members, readers, owners of journals, and publishers (medical and scientific journal community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for ethical and professional conduct in biomedical and scientific publishing, covering study design, data analysis, authorship, peer review, editorial duties, conflicts of interest, handling misconduct, media relations, advertising, and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design and ethical approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Good research should be well justified, well planned, appropriately designed, and ethically approved. To conduct research to a lower standard may constitute misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Laboratory and clinical research should be driven by protocol; pilot studies should have a written rationale. (2) Research protocols should seek to answer specific questions, rather than just collect data. (3) Protocols must be carefully agreed by all contributors and collaborators, including, if appropriate, the participants. (4) The final protocol should form part of the research record. (5) Early agreement on the precise roles of the contributors and collaborators, and on matters of authorship and publication, is advised. (6) Statistical issues should be considered early in study design, including power calculations, to ensure there are neither too few nor too many participants. (7) Formal and documented ethical approval from an appropriately constituted research ethics committee is required for all studies involving people, medical records, and anonymised human tissues. (8) Use of human tissues in research should conform to the highest ethical standards, such as those recommended by the Nuffield Council on Bioethics. (9) Fully informed consent should always be sought; where not possible an appropriately constituted research ethics committee should decide if this is ethically acceptable. (10) When participants are unable to give fully informed consent, research should follow international guidelines (e.g., CIOMS). (11) Animal experiments require full compliance with local, national, ethical, and regulatory principles and licensing arrangements. (12) Formal supervision (usually the principal investigator) should be provided for all research projects, including quality control, frequent review, and long-term retention (may be up to 15 years) of all records and primary outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Data should be appropriately analysed; fabrication and falsification constitute misconduct although inappropriate analysis alone does not necessarily amount to misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) All sources and methods used to obtain and analyse data, including any electronic pre-processing, should be fully disclosed; detailed explanations should be provided for any exclusions. (2) Methods of analysis must be explained in detail, and referenced if they are not in common use. (3) Post hoc analysis of subgroups is acceptable provided it is disclosed; failure to disclose that the analysis was post hoc is unacceptable. (4) The discussion should mention any issues of bias considered and explain how they were dealt with in design and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universally agreed definition of authorship; as a minimum, authors should take responsibility for a particular section of the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) The award of authorship should balance intellectual contributions to conception, design, analysis and writing against collection of data and routine work; if no reasonable task can be attributed, that individual should not be credited. (2) Decide early who will be credited as authors and who will be acknowledged to avoid disputes. (3) If professional writers employed by companies or agencies have written the paper, their names should be included and any conflicts of interest declared. (4) All authors must take public responsibility for the content of their paper; disclosure of individual contributions can help resolve multidisciplinary responsibility. (5) Careful reading of the target journal’s ‘Advice to Authors’ is advised. (6) Authors should be vigilant about allowing their name to be used to add credibility where inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest arise when authors, reviewers, or editors have interests not fully apparent that may influence judgments about what is published; they include personal, commercial, political, academic or financial interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial interests may include employment, research funding, stock/share ownership, payment for lectures or travel, consultancies and company support for staff. (1) Such interests, where relevant, must be declared to editors by researchers, authors, and reviewers. (2) Editors should also disclose relevant conflicts of interest to their readers; if in doubt, disclose. (3) Editors should consider disclosing conflicts of interest of their teams, editorial boards, managers, and owners. (4) Sometimes conflicts may be so extreme that publication is not possible or people must be excluded from decisions on publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers are external experts chosen by editors to provide written opinions with the aim of improving the study; procedures vary (e.g., open review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Suggestions from authors as to potential reviewers are often useful but editors are not obliged to use them. (2) The duty of confidentiality in manuscript assessment must be maintained by expert reviewers, and extends to colleagues asked for opinions (with editor’s permission). (3) The submitted manuscript should not be retained or copied. (4) Reviewers and editors should not make any use of the data, arguments, or interpretations unless they have authors’ permission. (5) Reviewers should provide speedy, accurate, courteous, unbiased and justifiable reports. (6) If reviewers suspect misconduct they should write in confidence to the editor. (7) Journals should publish accurate descriptions of their peer review selection and appeals processes. (8) Journals should provide regular audits of acceptance rates and publication times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundant publication occurs when two or more papers, without full cross reference, share the same hypothesis, data, discussion points, or conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Published studies do not need to be repeated unless further confirmation is required. (2) Previous publication of an abstract during meeting proceedings does not preclude later submission for publication, but full disclosure should be made at submission. (3) Re-publication in another language is acceptable provided there is full and prominent disclosure of the original source at submission. (4) At submission, authors should disclose details of related papers, even in different languages, and similar papers in press. (5) All original studies should be peer reviewed before publication, taking account of possible bias due to related or conflicting interests. (6) Editors must treat all submitted papers as confidential. (7) When a published paper is found to contain major flaws, editors must correct the record prominently and promptly. (8) Where misconduct is suspected, the editor must write to the authors first before contacting the head of the institution concerned. (9) Editors should ensure Instructions to Authors specify the need for authors to obtain informed consent from patients included in research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism ranges from unreferenced use of others’ published and unpublished ideas through submission under 'new' authorship of a complete paper; it can occur at any stage and applies to print and electronic versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) All sources should be disclosed, and if large amounts of other people’s written or illustrative material are to be used, permission must be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are the stewards of journals and must balance interests of readers, authors, staff, owners, editorial boards, advertisers and the media while providing direction and a strong management team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Editorial decisions to accept or reject should be based only on the paper’s importance, originality, clarity, and relevance to the remit of the journal. (2) Studies that challenge previous work published in the journal should be given an especially sympathetic hearing. (3) Studies reporting negative results should not be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical research findings attract media interest; premature mass-media publication of preliminary results can occur and must be managed responsibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Authors approached by media should give as balanced an account as possible, pointing out where evidence ends and speculation begins. (2) Simultaneous publication in mass media and a peer-reviewed journal is advised, as it usually means enough evidence/data have been provided. (3) Where simultaneous publication is not possible, authors should help journalists produce accurate reports but refrain from supplying additional data. (4) Patients who helped with research should be informed of results by authors before the mass media if there are clinical implications. (5) Authors should be advised by organisers if journalists will attend scientific meetings. (6) It may help authors to be advised of any media policies operated by the journal in which their work is to be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals and meetings derive significant income from advertising and reprints, but editorial independence must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Editorial decisions must not be influenced by advertising revenue or reprint potential: editorial and advertising administration must be clearly separated. (2) Advertisements that mislead must be refused, and editors must be willing to publish criticisms according to the same criteria used for other material in the journal. (3) Reprints should be published as they appear in the journal unless a correction is to be added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with misconduct — principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct is characterised by intention to cause others to regard as true that which is not true; investigation must focus on the act and the intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) The general principle confirming misconduct is intention to cause others to regard as true that which is not true. (2) Examination of misconduct must focus not only on the act or omission but also on the intention of those involved. (3) Deception may be by intention, reckless disregard, or negligence; best practice requires complete honesty and full disclosure. (4) Codes of practice raise awareness but can never be exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have an ethical obligation to pursue cases that raise questions of misconduct, but investigating and responding appropriately can be difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Editors should not simply reject papers that raise questions of misconduct; they are ethically obliged to pursue the case. (2) COPE can advise but for legal reasons only on anonymised cases. (3) It is for the editor to decide what action to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious misconduct — response
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious allegations require careful handling because editors often lack legal legitimacy or means to investigate; responses may require notifying employers, seeking expert advice, or referring cases to appropriate authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Editors must take allegations and suspicions seriously while recognizing their limits to investigate. (2) If accusations are not accompanied by convincing evidence, editors should confidentially seek expert advice. (3) If experts raise serious questions, editors should notify employers. (4) If experts find no evidence, editorial processes should proceed normally. (5) If convincing evidence of serious misconduct exists and there is no employer to refer to, and authors are registered doctors, cases can be referred to the General Medical Council. (6) If no organisation has legitimacy/means to investigate, the editor may decide the case warrants publishing something in the journal; legal advice will then be essential. (7) If editors believe an employer has not conducted an adequate investigation, publication of a notice in the journal may be warranted; legal advice is essential. (8) Authors should be given the opportunity to respond to accusations of serious misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less serious misconduct — response
rubrics_metrics.description: Less serious cases (redundant publication, deception over authorship, failure to declare conflicts) may be handled without involving employers, but implications for authors should be considered and fair procedures followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Editors may judge it unnecessary to involve employers in less serious cases, though appointing an independent expert may be wise. (2) Editors should remember accusations of even minor misconduct may have serious implications and it may be necessary to ask employers to investigate. (3) Authors should be given the opportunity to respond to any charge of minor misconduct. (4) If convinced of wrongdoing, editors may adopt sanctions (see sanctions list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible sanctions, ranked approximately by severity, that editors may apply for proven misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) A letter of explanation (and education) to the authors for genuine misunderstanding. (2) A letter of reprimand and warning as to future conduct. (3) A formal letter to the relevant head of institution or funding body. (4) Publication of a notice of redundant publication or plagiarism. (5) An editorial giving full details of the misconduct. (6) Refusal to accept future submissions from the individual, unit, or institution responsible, for a stated period. (7) Formal withdrawal or retraction of the paper from the literature, informing other editors and indexing authorities. (8) Reporting the case to the General Medical Council or other authority/organisation which can investigate and act with due process.
